ON THIS DAY — October 27, 1954: the Tuskegee commander pins on a general's star. 🇺🇸

Benjamin O. Davis Jr. was the son of the Army's first Black general — and a West Point cadet who endured four years of the "silent treatment," shunned by classmates who would not speak to him, in the hope he would quit. He graduated anyway, and when America finally let Black men fly, Davis took command of the Tuskegee Airmen — the 99th Fighter Squadron and then the 332nd Fighter Group, whose Red Tails guarded bombers over Europe and built one of the finest escort records of the war.

His reward for excellence, in a segregated Air Force, was to keep proving himself for another decade. Then, on October 27, 1954, the United States Air Force promoted Benjamin O. Davis Jr. to Brigadier General — the first African American general in the service's history.

He retired a Lieutenant General, and in 1998 President Bill Clinton advanced him to full four-star General. The cadet they tried to silence with silence outlasted them all.

During the Vietnam War, soldiers turned their helmets into a canvas for self-expression. Peace signs, personal messages, jokes, and countdowns to going home offered glimpses of their personalities, hopes, and humor. Each helmet carried a different story about the people living through the war.

The Thunderbirds had flown for half a century without a woman in the formation. Then came Nicole Malachowski. 🇺🇸

Nicole Malachowski caught the flying bug at age five, watching the Air Force Thunderbirds streak over an airshow — and spent the next two decades making sure she would be ready if the door ever opened.

It did. By then she was a combat-proven F-15E Strike Eagle pilot with missions over Iraq, a flight lead trusted with the lives of her wingmen. In 2005 the Thunderbirds announced their newest pilot: for the first time in the team's history, a woman — Malachowski would fly the Number 3 jet, right wing, inches from the leader at hundreds of miles an hour, for the 2006 and 2007 seasons.

She went on to command a fighter squadron and to serve at the White House. A tick-borne illness ended her flying career and nearly took her ability to walk and speak — so she fought that too, becoming a national voice for patients like her. Nicole Malachowski retired a Colonel, having spent a lifetime proving that "first" is not a finish line. It is an invitation to everyone behind you.

Japanese prosecutors have formally indicted 20-year-old U.S. Marine Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard on charges of robbery and murder following the death of a 39-year-old Japanese woman in Naha, Okinawa.

 Prosecutors from the Naha District Public Prosecutors Office allege that Ballard strangled the victim inside a hotel room in Naha on October 3 before fleeing with a backpack containing her wallet and personal belongings. If convicted under Japanese law, the charges carry penalties up to life imprisonment or capital punishment.

 Stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, Ballard was taken into custody by local police shortly after the incident. Leadership with the III Marine Expeditionary Force stated that the U.S. military recognizes the severity of the charges and will fully cooperate with Japanese legal authorities throughout the judicial process.

The case has triggered fierce local demonstrations outside government ministries and the U.S. Embassy, reigniting long-standing civic and political scrutiny over the heavy concentration of American military installations hosted across the island prefecture.

She was six years old when she decided to fly fighters. The Air Force had never had a Black woman fighter pilot. She fixed that. 🇺🇸

Shawna Rochelle Kimbrell set her course early — Civil Air Patrol at fourteen, an Air Force Academy appointment, and wings pinned on as a pilot with one goal in the jet that mattered most: the F-16 Fighting Falcon.

In 1998 she became the first African American woman fighter pilot in the history of the United States Air Force. She deployed to Turkey and flew combat air patrols over northern Iraq for Operation Northern Watch — watching over the no-fly zone from the cockpit she had dreamed about as a child — and later flew missions over South America and taught the next generation as an instructor pilot.

Kimbrell retired as a Lieutenant Colonel after a career of firsts, and spent her years after uniform doing what firsts are for: standing in front of young girls — especially girls who looked like her — and telling them the cockpit has a seat with their name on it too.

ESTES, JUSTIN M. (KIA)

Citation: The President of the United States takes pride in presenting the Silver Star Medal (Posthumously) to Justin M. Estes, Staff Sergeant, U.S. Army, for gallantry in action while serving with Company C, 2d Battalion, 505th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 3d Brigade Combat Team, 82d Airborne Division, in action on 5 March 2007 while on combat patrol operations during Operation Iraqi Freedom 06-08. Staff Sergeant Estes' instinctual actions and personal courage undoubtedly prevented a future attack on Coalition Forces, Iraqi Security Forces or innocent civilians at the cost of his own grievous injuries. Staff Sergeant Estes' actions are in keeping with the finest traditions of military heroism and reflect distinct credit upon him, Task Force 2d Battalion, 505th Parachute Infantry Regiment, Task Force Lightning, and the United States Army.

NARRATIVE TO ACCOMPANY AWARD:
Staff Sergeant Estes distinguished himself by conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty of 5 March 2007, while serving as a Squad Leader in 1st Platoon, Charlie Company, 2d Battalion, 505th Parachute Infantry Regiment, during a complex improvised explosive device (IED) attack in the city of Samarra, Iraq during Operation Iraqi Freedom 06-08. Staff Sergeant Estes' platoon was tasked with conducting reconnaissance of the berm on the eastern side of the volatile city of Samarra in order to prevent the flow of insurgent forces into the city. During the patrol, the lead HMMWV struck a pressure activated IED resulting in the catastrophic destruction of the vehicle, followed by a secondary command-detonated IED targeting the casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) team. Staff Sergeant Estes was the truck commander of the third truck in the patrol when the first IED was struck, placing him 100 meters behind the lead HMMWV to provide security for the patrol. The first IED engulfed the lead HMMWV in flames, leaving burning debris scattered around the detonation site. Five Paratroopers were injured in the blast, two of whom were thrown from the truck; they were still alive, but on fire and among the burning debris. Without hesitation and aware of the imminent danger posed not only by the flames and exploding ordnance, but also secondary IEDs, Staff Sergeant Estes grabbed the fire blanket and ran through the inferno surrounding the destroyed vehicle to render medical aid. Staff Sergeant Estes feverishly attempted to save the life of Staff Sergeant Stanley, providing medical care until the platoon medic arrived. Staff Sergeant Estes then took charge of the combat lifesaver team and began moving casualties out of the wreckage and flames for treatment. Staff Sergeant Estes provided calm and decisive leadership at the detonation site, directing the continuing search for Paratroopers affected by the blast, even as ammunition cooked off around him. Having cleared the casualties from the fire, and with his equipment literally melting from the intense heat, Staff Sergeant Estes remained at the side of Staff Sergeant Stanley as he called the stretcher teams forward to conduct CASEVAC. As the teams approached, the imminent danger at which Staff Sergeant Estes had placed himself in order to save the lives of his comrades was realized, as he was engulfed in a cloud of smoke and debris as a secondary IED detonated directly underneath his feet, killing him instantly. In an ultimate act of bravery and selfless service to his comrades in which he gave his own life, Staff Sergeant Estes attempted to save the lives of five of his comrades. By his undaunted courage, intrepid fighting spirit, and unwavering devotion to duty, Staff Sergeant Estes gallantly gave his life for his country, upholding the highest traditions of military heroism and reflecting distinct credit upon himself, Task Force Two Panther, Task Force Lightning, and the United States Army.

Twice wounded, he would not leave. A third wound finally stopped him — after the last position fell. 🇺🇸

On May 2, 1968, Captain James E. Livingston led Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines, in an assault on the fortified village of Dai Do in Vietnam's Quang Tri Province — one of the fiercest fights of the war.

Livingston charged at the head of his men from bunker to bunker. Wounded in the leg, he refused medical aid and kept attacking. When a sister company was pinned down and surrounded, he led a rescue force across open ground under murderous fire, was wounded a second and then a third time — and still refused evacuation until he had personally made sure every one of his wounded Marines was carried out first. Only then did he allow himself to be taken to the rear, collapsing from loss of blood.

President Richard Nixon presented him the Medal of Honor on May 14, 1970. James Livingston served more than thirty years, retiring as a Major General — and the Marines of Dai Do never forgot the captain who would not leave the field while a single one of his men remained on it.

After nearly 28 years of service in the U.S. Army, Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was serving in Afghanistan when his life ended unexpectedly. On February 3, 2012, the 49-year-old commander of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary) was found deceased in his quarters in Kabul. Officials said he appeared to have died of natural causes, not in combat. At the time, he was the highest-ranking American service member reported to have died during the Afghanistan War.

Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1962, Hildner grew up in a military family, moving between places including Japan, Italy, and Colorado. He graduated from the University of Notre Dame in 1984 and began his Army career as a commissioned officer.

His early assignments included service with the 3rd Armored Cavalry Regiment at Fort Bliss and the 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment in West Germany. He commanded a cavalry troop and took part in the final American patrol along the East-West German border before reunification.

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, Hildner and his troop deployed with the U.S. VII Corps during Operation Desert Storm. He later moved into Army logistics, taking on the vital work of making sure troops had the supplies, equipment, and support needed to carry out their missions.

In 2003, he led the Special Troops Battalion of the 13th Corps Support Command at Fort Hood. The unit deployed to Iraq, supporting U.S. forces near Joint Base Balad and Abu Ghraib, and later assisted with relief operations after Hurricane Katrina. From 2007 to 2009, he commanded the 23rd Quartermaster Brigade at Fort Lee, which trained more than 20,000 soldiers each year.

In 2010, Hildner assumed command of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary). The following year, he deployed to Afghanistan as deputy commander for support operations with NATO Training Mission–Afghanistan. His work included helping Afghan leaders build systems to supply and maintain their security forces.

His death in Kabul brought profound grief to his family and the soldiers who served with him. His father, Robert, told The Washington Post that he believed Terence may have suffered a heart attack; this was a family member’s belief, not a confirmed medical finding. Army accounts described the death as due to natural causes. No enemy attack or combat injury was reported.

Hildner was survived by his wife, Cindy, their four children, his parents, and his siblings. His father remembered him for his humor, determination, and analytical mind. On February 29, 2012, he was laid to rest with military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.

His decorations included the Legion of Merit, two Bronze Star Medals, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, and the Combat Action Badge—honors earned over a career that spanned multiple conflicts and senior leadership roles.

His story is a reminder that service members can be lost overseas not only in combat, but also to illness and other non-combat circumstances. Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was a husband, father, son, and dedicated Army officer whose service ended far from home.

Rest peacefully, General Hildner. Your commitment to your soldiers and family will not be forgotten.

He had a way out. The four men below him did not. Ross McGinnis was nineteen. 🇺🇸

On December 4, 2006, Private First Class Ross McGinnis of the 1st Battalion, 26th Infantry, was manning the gun turret of a Humvee rolling through the Adhamiyah district of Baghdad when an insurgent on a rooftop dropped a grenade straight into the vehicle.

McGinnis shouted a warning. There was time for one decision. As the turret gunner, he alone had a clear path to jump clear and save himself — instead, he dropped down into the Humvee and threw his body over the live grenade, pinning it between his back and the radio mount. The explosion took his life and spared all four men in the vehicle below him, who walked away with only minor wounds.

He was nineteen years old, from Knox, Pennsylvania — remembered by his crew as the soldier who was always smiling. On June 2, 2008, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor to Ross McGinnis's parents at the White House. Four men went home to their families because a nineteen-year-old chose them over himself.

He fought on alone for over an hour after everyone believed he was gone — and the camera in the sky proved it. 🇺🇸

On March 4, 2002, on the snow-covered peak of Takur Ghar in Afghanistan, Technical Sergeant John Chapman — a U.S. Air Force Combat Controller attached to a Navy SEAL team — went back up the mountain to rescue a fallen teammate.

Dropped into an ambush, Chapman charged straight uphill into an enemy bunker and k*lled its fighters at point-blank range. Wounded and bleeding, he charged a second position to draw fire away from the rescue helicopter coming for his team. The SEALs, believing him d*ad, were forced to withdraw.

But John Chapman was not gone. Years later, painstaking analysis of surveillance footage revealed he had regained consciousness and fought on alone for more than an hour — engaging enemy fighters hand to hand — until he was finally k*lled standing in the open, drawing fire away from an incoming rescue force. His was the first Medal of Honor action in history to be captured on camera.

In 2018, President Donald Trump presented Chapman's Medal of Honor to his widow, Valerie — making him the first U.S. airman to receive the award since the Vietnam War, and finally giving him the recognition his final hour deserved.

WYCKOFF, CHARLES (KIA)

Citation: The President of the United States takes pride in presenting the Distinguished Service Cross (Posthumously) to Charles Wyckoff, Sergeant, U.S. Army, for extraordinary heroism in action while serving with the 3d Platoon, Company C, 1st Battalion, 508th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 3d Brigade Combat Team, 82d Airborne Division. On 6 June 2007, Sergeant Wyckoff distinguished himself as a Rifle Team Leader in combat operations during Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. While engaged in close combat against determined enemy forces, Sergeant Wyckoff left his covered position without hesitation, to force the other members of his team to take cover. Sergeant Wyckoff revealed his position and fatally engaged two insurgents to save the lives of his platoon. Sergeant Wyckoff's bravery is in keeping with the finest traditions of military service and reflects great credit upon himself, the 82d Airborne Division and the United States Army.

The U.S. Army has officially begun integrating counter-unmanned aerial systems (C-UAS) air-to-air combat training into its AH-64 Apache flight curriculum, preparing pilots to hunt and destroy Iranian-style Shahed one-way attack drones.

 With low-flying, slow-speed loitering munitions proving difficult for traditional high-altitude air defense radars to track, rotary-wing gunships are stepping into a vital mobile defense role to plug gaps across contested airspace.

 Firing multi-million-dollar surface-to-air missiles at inexpensive kamikaze drones drains vital stockpiles; the Apache leverages precision 30mm M230 chain guns, APKWS laser-guided rockets, and advanced electro-optical sensors to neutralize drone threats at a fraction of the cost.

Recent live-fire demonstrations and multinational exercises across Europe and the Middle East have seen AH-64E crews successfully detect, track, and shoot down simulated one-way attack drones in dynamic air-to-air engagements.

It was his 25th birthday. His gift to his men was walking into the house of death alone. 🇺🇸

On November 10, 2004, in the savage street fighting of Fallujah, Staff Sergeant David Bellavia's platoon from the 1st Infantry Division was ambushed inside a block of houses. Taking fire from a fortified room, his squad was pinned down and about to be overrun.

Bellavia traded his weapon for a squad automatic rifle and stormed the house alone. In total darkness he moved room to room, engaging insurgent after insurgent at arm's length — at one point fighting an enemy fighter hand to hand — until the house was clear and his men were safe. His lone assault saved his entire squad.

For years, David Bellavia was the only living Medal of Honor recipient of the Iraq War who had not yet received the medal. That changed on June 25, 2019, when President Donald Trump placed it around his neck at the White House. Bellavia used the moment the way he has used every moment since: to name and honor the soldiers of his unit who never came home, the men he wrote about in his book "House to House."

In 1962, fifty men were chosen to become the first Navy SEALs. One of them made history just by standing in the line. 🇺🇸

When President Kennedy's call created the Navy SEALs, Master Chief William Goines was there at the very beginning — a plank owner of SEAL Team Two and the only African American among the original SEALs.

Goines had enlisted in 1955, inspired by the Navy frogmen he had seen as a boy. Trained as a parachutist, demolitions expert and master swimmer, he made three combat tours to Vietnam, led men in the Teams for decades, and helped shape the traditions every SEAL still follows today — retiring in 1990 after 32 years of service as a Master Chief.

After the uniform came a schoolhouse: Goines served his Ohio community as a school resource officer and police chief, still protecting people, still leading from the front. When he died on June 10, 2024, at 87, the SEAL community mourned one of its founding fathers — a man who opened a door that generations of warriors have walked through since.

William Goines was not just among the first. In every way that matters, he was a first.

On this day, October 26, 2009, 29-year-old U.S. Marine Corps AH-1W Super Cobra pilot Capt. Kyle R. Van De Giesen of Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron 169 ("Vipers") made the ultimate sacrifice while flying combat operations in Helmand Province, Afghanistan.

A former standout quarterback from North Attleborough, Massachusetts, who left behind a young daughter and pregnant wife, Capt. Van De Giesen fell alongside fellow Marine aviators Capt. David S. Mitchell, Capt. Eric A. Jones, and Cpl. Gregory M.W. Fleury while providing overhead fire support for Marines on the ground.

Semper Fidelis, Capt. Van De Giesen. Never forgotten. 🇺🇸🦅🌎

Confronting the challenges presented by the unconventional war in Iraq, Air Force Technical Sergeant Shawn Foust was assigned to Joint Logistic Task Force 1144, becoming a Convoy Commander for the 424th Medium Truck Detachment. In 212 missions during his second tour of duty, Foust encountered various obstacles and challenges while amassing over 507,000 cumulative miles on the dangerous roads of Iraq.

Convoy mission 57-459 would present the greatest challenge, earning Foust praise for his ability to overcome such a daunting task. As his convoy was approaching Forward Operating Base Al Asad, a roadside bomb detonated, wounding the driver and passenger of the third truck, and leaving the vehicle partially disabled. A possible full-scale ambush was upon them as scattered mortar and small arms fire landed on their position. The intermittent insurgent fire raised the threat level for the entire convey and Foust knew he had to remain calm and professional.

He immediately moved the convoy past the kill zone and went back for the wounded men. Foust organized his Airmen into a defensive posture, and prepared to repair the damaged truck. Working tirelessly and on constant guard for six hours, throughout the night, Foust and his fifteen man squad replaced each of the damaged 250 pound tires until the vehicle was operational. Foust successfully completed this mission all those before and all those that followed.

In the six months he spent in Iraq, he exhibited a sense of service, devotion to duty, and commitment to the overall success of his unit that went above and beyond what was expected, earning him the Bronze Star Medal for exceptionally meritorious service.

Today, October 26, is National Day of the Deployed—a day to honor every American soldier, sailor, airman, Marine, Guardian, and Coast Guardsman currently standing the watch far from home, as well as the families holding down the front at home until they return.

From carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea and forward outposts across the Middle East to airbases in the Indo-Pacific and patrols along Eastern Europe, hundreds of thousands of U.S. service members are on station right now so the rest of us can sleep in peace.

UK defense leadership has issued a stark, high-priority warning emphasizing that Britain and its NATO allies must rapidly accelerate their military readiness and national resilience.

The 2030 Horizon: Citing the rapid expansion of adversary force strengths and wartime industrial output, defense officials stressed that potential threats could mature significantly by 2030, leaving a narrow window of roughly 1,000 days to ensure forces are fully prepared to fight and win.

Rebuilding National Resilience: Beyond front-line military modernization, the push includes enhancing civil defense preparedness, securing critical supply chains, and reinforcing infrastructure against cyber and hybrid threats.

Deterrence Through Strength: The overarching message emphasizes that preventing future large-scale conflict requires immediate, decisive reinvestment in defense capabilities while there is still time to deter potential aggression.

"Capt. Derek Herrera had vowed to leave the Marine Corps the same way he entered it: on his own feet. Aided by robotic leg braces, this Marine, paralyzed from the chest down by a sniper in Afghanistan, walked across a parade ground at Camp Pendleton to receive a Bronze Star for bravery. Herrera, 30, a Naval Academy graduate, is set to retire next week. He is studying for an MBA at UCLA and plans to become involved in helping veterans. "Your drive and determination are great and you will continue to do great things," Lt. Col. John Lynch told Herrera. Some 300 Marines and other guests watched in respectful silence as Herrera, his wife Maura, and his service dog Shaggy arrived at the ceremony. The only sound was the soft whirring of the robotic system's motors. Herrera is the first person in the country to purchase a ReWalk system, according to the manufacturer, ReWalk Robotics Ltd."(@USMarineCorps photo by Sgt. Scott Achtemeier)

SOCOM is pushing for a radically lighter 10-lb 5.56mm light machine gun to supercharge operator mobility.

U.S. Special Operations Command is driving a hard modernization effort to replace the legacy Mk 46 light machine gun with an entirely new weapon system known as the Flyweight Assault Machine Gun (FAMG).

When command operators are moving fast across unforgiving terrain on direct-action raids, every single ounce counts. Traditional squad automatic weapons provide immense sustained firepower, but the physical weight of hauling a heavy gun and hundreds of rounds of linked ammunition can severely slow down a dismounted element.

SOCOM's strict requirements outline a weapon with a target weight of just 10 pounds (and no more than 11.5 pounds with its standard rail interface, bipod, and carry handle), drastically cutting down the load carried by front-line commandos.

Chambered in standard 5.56x45mm NATO, the new belt-fed machine gun is engineered to feature a maximum length of 39 inches, a side-folding collapsible stock, and a quick-change barrel that can be swapped out in under 30 seconds.

 With prototype testing and development moving forward under the U.S. Navy's NSWC Crane, SOCOM plans to award a production contract and begin fielding the new weapon to operators by fiscal year 2028.

A striking combat perspective shows a rifleman with the 2nd Battalion, 6th Marine Regiment (2/6 "The Ready Battalion") maintaining visual contact through his optic during extreme cold-weather operations in Setermoen, Norway.   

Operating in the freezing wilderness of Setermoen, Marines from 2/6 undergo rigorous cold-weather training and tactical maneuver drills With the strategic importance of the Arctic corridor and NATO's northern flank reaching historic highs, rapid winter deployments ensure the Marine Corps maintains instant, forward-deployed combat overmatch in any climate. honing their combat effectiveness to operate seamlessly alongside NATO allies under unforgiving sub-zero conditions. 

Outfitted in arctic overwhites to disappear into snow-blanketed timberline terrain, infantrymen must manage everything from weapon lubrication and deep-freeze battery drains to survival mobility where the environment itself can be as lethal as enemy fire.

The U.S. Army takes delivery of its first mobile tactical cannon prototype to replace the aging M777 howitzer.

As the military shifts away from towed artillery systems toward highly mobile, survivable platforms, the U.S. Army has officially taken delivery of its first wheeled Mobile Tactical Cannon prototype built by Hanwha Defense USA.

Based on a wheeled variant of the combat-proven K9 Thunder self-propelled artillery, the new 155mm system features a 52-caliber barrel designed to offer significantly extended range and rapid "shoot-and-scoot" mobility.

The prototyping effort is backed by an agreement worth up to approximately $263 million covering initial prototypes and testing options, with full fielding targeted by 2031.

Moving away from traditional towed platforms like the M777—which require heavy vehicles to tow them and leave crews vulnerable to counter-battery fire—the new wheeled howitzers are designed to integrate heavily with brigade combat teams for modern high-intensity warfare.

How U.S. Marine Kyle Carpenter stared death in the face, threw himself on a grenade, and lived to earn the Medal of Honor.

On November 21, 2010, Lance Corporal Kyle Carpenter and a fellow Marine were manning a rooftop security post in the volatile Helmand Province of Afghanistan. Stationed in a small village to disrupt enemy activity and protect local residents, they suddenly found themselves targeted in a daylight Taliban attack. Without warning, an enemy hand grenade was hurled directly into their sandbagged position.

What happened next was an act of raw, instinctual selflessness that defies human logic. Without a second thought and with complete disregard for his own safety, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his body directly over the live explosive to shield his best friend from the blast.

When the grenade detonated, Carpenter absorbed the devastating brunt of the shrapnel and concussive force. The injuries were catastrophic: his right arm was shattered, his jaw was broken, he lost his right eye, and medical personnel initially flatlined him three times as he fought for his life. He endured a five-week coma, brain surgery, and nearly 40 grueling surgeries over nearly three years of intense rehabilitation.

Against all medical odds, Carpenter survived. In 2014, he received the Medal of Honor from President Barack Obama, becoming the youngest living recipient of the nation's highest military decoration. Since his medical retirement, he has gone on to run marathons, write a book, and inspire millions by turning his scars into a testament of resilience.

What are your thoughts on the extraordinary sacrifice of warriors who willingly lay down their lives so their brothers can make it home?

He fought all night in his socks, in the snow, throwing back live grenades with his bare hands. 🇺🇸

On the night of November 28, 1950, at the Toktong Pass near the Chosin Reservoir in Korea, Private First Class Hector Cafferata of Fox Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, was asleep when a Chinese force of regimental size smashed into the Marine line.

Cafferata ran to the fight without even stopping for his boots. Through hours of darkness, he and Private Kenneth Benson held their stretch of the line almost alone — Cafferata firing into the waves of attackers, catching live enemy grenades in mid-action and hurling them back, one exploding so close it tore the flesh from his fingers. When Benson was blinded by a grenade blast, Cafferata fought on for both of them, shielding his friend while still manning the position until daylight and reinforcements broke the attack.

For that night, Hector Cafferata received the Medal of Honor from President Truman. He spent the rest of his life insisting he was no hero — that the real heroes were the Marines who never came home from that frozen pass.

He died on April 12, 2016, at 86 years old — a man who once held a mountain pass in his stocking feet.

Chief Warrant Officer Carlos M. Roman, a native of Fayetteville, N.C., has been awarded a Distinguished Flying Cross by Maj. Gen. James L. Huggins, the commanding general of the 82nd Airborne Division, at Simmons Army Airfield, March 14, 2011.

Newly released Pentagon UFO files recount FBI agents’ report of a mysterious black triangle hovering above a mountain ridge before disappearing within seconds. The brief encounter was documented, but the object’s identity and sudden vanishing remain unexplained.

On this day, October 25, 1983, U.S. Army Capt. Keith J. Lucas of Task Force 160 became the first "Night Stalker" killed in combat in the history of the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment during the opening hours of Operation Urgent Fury in Grenada.

Tasked with inserting Delta Force operators into the heavily fortified Richmond Hill Prison in broad daylight, Capt. Lucas flew his UH-60 Black Hawk through blistering anti-aircraft and heavy machine-gun fire—setting the standard for the motto Night Stalkers Don't Quit that every 160th SOAR aviator carries into battle today.

Wounded on the first day, wounded again on the third — on the fourth day, he gave his life to break the ambush. 🇺🇸

Sergeant Alfredo "Freddy" Gonzalez of Edinburg, Texas, led a platoon of Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 1st Marines, into the street fighting of Hue City during the Tet Offensive of 1968.

On January 31 he was hit by enemy fire while carrying a wounded Marine to safety — and refused evacuation. On February 3, mortar fragments tore into him again — and still he stayed. On February 4, his company was pinned down by a fortified machine-gun position in a church complex that nothing could crack. Gonzalez grabbed light anti-tank weapons and moved through the open, position after position, firing rocket after rocket until he had silenced the guns — struck down, mortally wounded, as his final rockets destroyed the strongpoint.

He was 21 years old. Vice President Spiro Agnew presented the Medal of Honor to Gonzalez's mother, Dolia, in 1969. The guided-missile destroyer USS Gonzalez sails today with his name on its stern — and in Edinburg, schools, streets and a generation of Texas Marines still grow up on the story of Freddy Gonzalez.

Marcus Luttrell, Navy Cross Recipient

Marcus Luttrell (born November 7, 1975) is a former United States Navy SEAL who received the Navy Cross and Purple Heart for his actions in June 2005 facing Taliban fighters during Operation Red Wings. Luttrell was a Hospital Corpsman First Class by the end of his eight-year career in the United States Navy.

He was deployed to Afghanistan in 2005 with SEAL Team Ten as part of SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team One (SDV-1).[4] While in Afghanistan, he was involved in Operation Red Wings, during which the four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SDV-1 was discovered by local herdsmen, subsequently ambushed, and all killed except for Luttrell. Luttrell was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during the operation. The team knew the local herdsmen might reveal their whereabouts to Taliban fighters but because they were not armed combatants, they were allowed to leave despite the risk to themselves and their mission.

The ambush during Operation Red Wings was intense. The four SEALs were attacked from three sides, and included fire from PK machine guns, AK-47s, RPG-7s, and 82mm mortars. The attack forced the SEALs into the northeast gulch of the Shuryek Valley side of Sawtalo Sar. The SEALs made a number of attempts to contact their combat operations center with a PRC-148 MBITR (Multi Band Inter/Intra Team Radio) and then with an Iridium Satellite Phone. They could not establish consistent communication, however, other than for a period long enough to indicate that they were under attack. Three of the four team members were killed, and Luttrell, being the only survivor, was left unconscious with a number of fractures, a broken back, and numerous shrapnel wounds. Members of SEAL Team 10 attempted a rescue during the firefight but their helicopter was shot down and all aboard were killed. Luttrell regained consciousness and evaded the pursuing enemy with the help of local Pashtun villagers, who eventually sent an emissary to the nearest U.S. base to secure his safe rescue and ultimately save his life. After recovering from his injuries, he returned to active duty and deployed to Ramadi during Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2006 as part of SEAL Team Five. He later had his knees blown out and fractured his spine again. This ultimately led to his discharge.

On this day, October 25, 2007, 22-year-old U.S. Army Sgt. Joshua C. Brennan of Battle Company, 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment (Airborne), 173rd Airborne Brigade Combat Team, was killed in action in the Korengal Valley, Afghanistan.

Known across his platoon for always volunteering to walk point without hesitation, Sgt. Brennan was leading his team along "Honcho Hill" when Taliban fighters sprung an L-shaped ambush from 30 feet away (The American Legion). When two insurgents tried to drag the wounded Brennan into the darkness, his best friend Staff Sgt. Salvatore Giunta charged through a wall of gunfire and killed one insurgent to bring Brennan back to his brothers—an action that earned Giunta the first living Medal of Honor since Vietnam (The American Legion, The American Presidency Project).

On this day, October 25, 2007, 29-year-old U.S. Army Combat Medic Spc. Hugo V. "Doc" Mendoza of Battle Company, 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment (Airborne), 173rd Airborne Brigade Combat Team, made the ultimate sacrifice in the Korengal Valley, Afghanistan (The American Legion, The American Presidency Project).

When his platoon was hit by a point-blank Taliban ambush in the dark, "Doc" Mendoza did what combat medics have always done—he ran straight toward the gunfire to reach his wounded brothers at the front of the patrol, giving his own life to save theirs (The American Legion).

Staff Sgt. Carlo A. Alcazar, Sgt. 1st Class Drew C. Kimmey, and Capt. Stephen P. Ward, members of Civil Affairs Team 745, were recently recognized for their performance during an Afghanistan mission last November. The three soldiers were recognized for rescuing a Special Forces team leader, also the ground forces commander that day.

CA Team 745 was stationed at Firebase Cobra in Oruzgan, Afghanistan, with special operations detachments from the 3rd Special Forces Group, members of the Afghan National Army, and the Afghan National Police. On Nov. 2, 2007, the teams and their Afghan counterparts left the firebase to visit the village of Sarsina to conduct a medical capabilities mission and a humanitarian aid drop. Once they arrived at the village, they discovered it had been evacuated and that Taliban fighters were entrenched in several fighting positions in an attempt to ambush forces in the area.

Alcazar reported only three families came in for medical treatment. The families told the soldiers the Taliban made the other people leave the village, but that having nowhere to go. they stayed. “What was alarming,” Ward said later, “was the buildings had locks and barricaded doors, which was a clear indication that the village wasn't abandoned, but had been turned into a defendable position.”

All three quickly figured it was only a matter of time before the firefight would begin.
The teams were quickly engaged by 300 Taliban fighters. According to Army documents, after an hour of fighting, two vehicles were pulled to the rear of the fight after being disabled. This left the ground forces commander to the front of the coalition lines and in jeopardy of being overrun. At this point, Ward, the team leader for 745, radioed to the ground forces commander, who was pinned down in a vulnerable building, that his was on its way. Ward later said he and Alcazar went because they were the closest truck and the others were busy providing cover. Unfortunately, the team's vehicle crashed into an enemy fighting position and became immobile, knocking Ward and Alcazar momentarily unconscious.
After they regained consciousness, Alcazar took to reloading ammunition belts, enabling Kimmey, the gunner, to continue to engage enemy forces. Ward exited the vehicle and directed his team to dismount and move to cover. Kimmey remained in the turret, providing cover for the team and allowing them to reach the ground forces commander. He stayed even though he knew the enemy was setting up mortar positions to destroy the truck he was firing from.

Kimmey was able to keep the Taliban from overrunning the soldiers with the .50-caliber gun. In the process, he was drawing a majority of the enemy fire. Ward reported the enemy was about 50 to 100 meters away at this point.

Team 745 moved to the ground commander's position and helped in the recovery of the commander and the casualties. All of this was done, while under “continual, accurate and effective” enemy fire.

Since the team's 745's vehicle was immobile, it was stripped of all sensitive equipment, and its gun was dismantled to prevent the enemy from gaining off of the team's loss. Once team 745 sterilized their truck, they had no choice but to run beside the Special Forces vehicle, using it as cover, until they reached safety, because there was no room for them on the truck. All three of them ran alongside the truck until they reached a checkpoint and mounted up into another vehicle for the ride back to Firebase Cobra.

During the civil affairs award ceremony, all three were honored for their heroic acts. Maj. Gen. John F. Mulholland, said, “The words can't do justice, nor can the medal on your chest convey what they went up against.”

On this day, 84 years ago, October 25, 1942, 40-year-old Private Percival Eric Gratwick faced heavy enemy fire during the Second Battle of El Alamein in Egypt.

Before enlisting, Gratwick worked as a gold prospector and station hand in the remote Pilbara region of Western Australia.

He served in the 2/48th Infantry Battalion, a unit that became Australia's most decorated battalion of World War II, earning four Victoria Crosses in total.

On the night of October 25, his company launched an attack on Trig 29 along Miteiriya Ridge.

Intense machine-gun and mortar fire from German and Italian positions pinned down Gratwick's platoon in open terrain.

Enfilade fire quickly killed the platoon commander, the platoon sergeant, and most of the men, leaving only seven survivors.

Recognizing that remaining pinned down meant total destruction, Gratwick acted on his own initiative.

He collected hand grenades, stood up into the line of fire, and charged the nearest enemy mortar position alone.

He reached the trench, threw his grenades, and killed the entire mortar crew.

With that position destroyed, Gratwick spotted a second enemy machine-gun post hurling heavy fire at his advancing company.

Armed only with his rifle and fixed bayonet, he immediately ran across open ground toward the machine gun.

He closed the distance under direct fire, charging into close-quarters combat and inflicting casualties on the defenders.

As he reached striking distance of the gun, a burst of machine-gun fire struck Gratwick, killing him instantly.

His solo attack destroyed key strongpoints and rattled the surviving enemy defenders.

Inspired by his charge, the rest of the company advanced, cleared the remaining enemy positions, and captured the final objective.

Gratwick had celebrated his 40th birthday just six days before giving his life in the assault.

On January 28, 1943, the British Crown posthumously awarded Private Percival Eric Gratwick the Victoria Cross.

He was buried at the El Alamein War Cemetery in Egypt at Plot XXII, Row A, Grave 6.

His mother accepted the Victoria Cross on his behalf, and the medal is now displayed at the Army Museum of Western Australia in Fremantle.

Ramadi, 2006. The most dangerous city on Earth — and this SEAL officer led from the front of it. 🇺🇸

Leif Babin served as a Navy SEAL officer with SEAL Team Three, deploying to Ramadi, Iraq, in 2006 as a platoon commander in Task Unit Bruiser — the most decorated special operations unit of the Iraq War. Under his task unit commander, Jocko Willink, Babin led his platoon through relentless urban combat in a city the enemy was determined to hold.

Babin was awarded the Silver Star, a Bronze Star and the Purple Heart for his service in that fight, where his platoon helped turn the tide in Anbar Province alongside American soldiers, Marines and brave Iraqi forces.

But his most famous battle began after the war. In 2015, Babin and Willink published "Extreme Ownership," the leadership book built entirely on the hard lessons of Ramadi — that there are no bad teams, only bad leaders, and that a leader owns everything in his world. The book became a phenomenon read in boardrooms, locker rooms and military units around the globe.

Through their company Echelon Front, Babin still teaches the same principle he proved in combat: leadership is everything.

The 23rd and 24th of June 2006 would be a crucible of leadership and heroism for an already battle-tested and decorated captain in the U.S. Army's Special Forces. Captain Sheffield F. Ford III was in charge of some 16 Americans and 46 Afghan Army soldiers during "Operation Kaika" in the Panjawi District of Afghanistan's Kandahar province.

In the bleak farmland, crisscrossed by ditches and barren expanses, Ford led his unit to "re-establish order" in the contested region, entering a Spartan Afghan village on the 23rd. The dilapidated buildings and mud huts were hiding a Taliban force of unknown strength with one thought on their minds: killing Americans and the Afghan soldiers working to take back their country. In their hastily prepared patrol base, Ford organized a perimeter as night enveloped the isolated Special Forces team and their Afghan allies.

As darkness fell, "all hell [broke] loose." From three directions, rifle, machine gun, and rocket-propelled grenade fire landed and exploded on their position. One of Ford's squad mates later said they had "not seen this disciplined execution of infantry tactics" by the Taliban. Ford dug his men in to repel the assault.

Moving from position to position, he alternated between barking orders, firing at the enemy, and rallying the Afghan soldiers with him. As the night crept on, the remaining Taliban fighters withdrew and Ford took stock of the situation.

Early the next day, he ordered some of his Special Forces operators to lead a team of Afghans into the suspected Taliban hideout. As the unit engaged the hostiles, it was divided in two when some 200 Taliban fighters poured out, separating the American attackers and surrounding the make-shift patrol base.

Over the radio, Ford was connected with one of the translators who had been leading the mission on the Taliban position. The translator saw two Americans were fighting despite being severely wounded and feared capture at any minute. Knowing the ramifications of being taken alive by the Taliban, the translator told Ford he would, if ordered, end the suffering of the troops and his own life rather than be captured. Ford responded, "We've got people coming." Ford organized and launched an effective rescue to recover the translator and wounded troops, even if they were mortally wounded. He would not allow American or Afghan alike to be taken in any condition by the Taliban.

The adversaries fought so close to one another that the terrorists screamed to the Afghan soldiers that, "we can forgive you; just put your weapons down and walk away. We want the Americans alive." The months of training and the ties formed between the Americans and the Afghans were put to the test. Seeing the example of Ford running to each of the beleaguered fighters in the face of constant fire, and remembering all they had endured alongside their American trainers, the Afghan soldiers responded to the Taliban's offer with well-aimed shots and an unbreakable defense.

Exemplifying the U.S. Special Forces motto, De Opresso Liber (to liberate the oppressed), Ford inspired his Afghan troops to stand up to the Taliban fighters and bring them down. He led an evacuation of all the men under his command, wounded included, out of the village under the cover of Apache attack choppers to ensure all would be safe while sealing the fate of the insurgents. Ford successfully extricated his men, and the unit had more than 120 confirmed kills. Just as the Americans and Afghans had trained together, they sacrificed together; two American and three Afghan soldiers would not leave the battlefield alive. For his accomplishments in the face of such an overpowering force, Ford was awarded the Silver Star, the nation's third highest military award.

Commander Rorke Denver spent his career the way SEALs prefer it: quietly. As an officer with SEAL Team Three, he led platoons on combat deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, earning the Bronze Star with Valor for his leadership under fire.

No actors pretending — the men on screen jumping from planes, clearing rooms and kicking in doors were the real warriors, performing live-fire tactics. Denver's face became, for millions of Americans, the face of the modern SEAL.

After hanging up his uniform, he put his story on paper in his book "Damn Few: Making the Modern SEAL Warrior," an honest look at what it takes to earn the Trident and carry its burden.

His philosophy is simple and famous among the Teams: calm is contagious — and so is panic. A leader's job is to bring the calm.

Hector A. Cafferata Jr. was a United States Marine Corps private who received the Medal of Honor for his extraordinary heroism during the Battle of Chosin Reservoir in the Korean War. In November 1950, Cafferata single-handedly held off a regimental-strength enemy force for hours in sub-zero temperatures, fighting in his socks and a light jacket without his boots or parka. He killed over 100 enemy combatants, swatted away a dozen live grenades with an entrenching tool, and ultimately sacrificed a finger and severely wounded his arm to hurl away a live grenade that landed among his wounded comrades. He survived the battle, was awarded the nation's highest military honor by President Harry S. Truman in 1952, and lived a quiet life until his passing in 2016.

BOADA, STEPHEN J., SILVER STAR RECIPIENT

Citation: The President of the United States takes pleasure in presenting the Silver Star Medal to Stephen J. Boada, First Lieutenant, U.S. Marine Corps, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action against the enemy while serving as Forward Observer and Forward Air Controller, Company K, Third Battalion, Third Marines, U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Central Command in support of Combined Joint Task Force-76 and Operation ENDURING FREEDOM from 5 to 9 May 2005. While operating near Shatagal Village, First Lieutenant Boada's platoon received intelligence that Al Qaeda and Associate Movement fighters were setting up an ambush position from which to attack the platoon upon their departure from Shatagal. Despite the barrage of intense enemy fire, he calmly directed the tactical employment of the unit and directed fires from an A-10 aircraft onto enemy positions. During the ensuing firefight, First Lieutenant Boada and members of his squad were wounded. Ignoring his injuries, he continued to fearlessly lead his Marines as they fought off a tenacious enemy while other members of the unit extracted their fallen comrades. As the platoon maneuvered over five kilometers of arduous mountain terrain with the injured Marines, First Lieutenant Boada called for and directed AC-130 aircraft to cover the unit's movement. This action resulted in the destruction of the besieging enemy. Without question, First Lieutenant Boada's tactical acumen in directing these aircraft saved many lives in the platoon as the enemy's ambush positions controlled the high ground through the terrain in which the platoon was conducting its retrograde. By his bold leadership, wise judgment, and complete dedication to duty, First Lieutenant Boada reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service.

Every legend has a first name. In the history of the Navy SEALs, that name is Harry Beal. 🇺🇸

Harry M. Beal was a coal miner's son from Meyersdale, Pennsylvania — just five feet tall, but able to do a pull-up with one arm. He enlisted in the Navy in 1948, and in 1955 he volunteered for the Underwater Demolition Teams, the legendary "frogmen" who swam ashore ahead of invasions to blow up mines and obstacles. It was some of the most dangerous work in the Navy — and Beal loved it.

In January 1962, President John F. Kennedy created the Navy SEALs — and when the call went out for volunteers to form the first teams, Harry Beal was the very first man to raise his hand. He became a plank owner of SEAL Team Two at Little Creek, Virginia. And because the Navy lists its men alphabetically, his name — Beal — stood first in the graduation book of the first SEAL class in history. Literally, the first name in SEAL history.

Weeks later, on February 20, 1962, Beal was aboard the destroyer USS Noa when astronaut John Glenn's capsule Friendship 7 splashed down after America's first orbital flight — and it was Harry Beal who personally helped pull Glenn from the capsule.

He went on to serve as an M-60 door gunner and a demolitions instructor, passing his hard-earned knowledge to the generations of SEALs who followed. He retired in 1968 after 20 years of service, then worked 20 more years for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation. His hometown named a bridge after him.

Harry Beal died on January 26, 2021, at the age of 90. He was not the biggest man or the strongest man. He was simply the first to step forward — and every SEAL who has ever raised his hand since has followed in his wake.

When two Rangers were critically wounded and lying in the open on a rooftop, Sergeant Peter Cimpoes immediately climbed a ladder into the kill zone to engage the enemy and protect the casualties. Less than 5 meters away, Cimpoes battled with 3 insurgents who were one story above him, firing down from an adjacent building. He drove the enemy behind cover long enough to drag the two wounded soldiers to safety and continued returning fire while others brought them off the roof. He tossed several grenades as well, silencing the enemy and shifting the momentum for a follow-up assault by the Rangers. His heroic actions allowed the successful retrieval of both casualties. One of the wounded Rangers, Sergeant Thomas MacPherson, died from his wounds. For his bravery, Cimpoes was awarded the Silver Star.

Sergeant Kendra Coleman joined the Army in 2007 and deployed to Afghanistan in 2009 as an MP, after earning her Airborne wings as a paratrooper.

On April 4, 2010, Coleman was riding in a vehicle when it hit an IED. She suffered traumatic brain injury and hearing loss from the explosion. Rather than be sent to Germany for treatment, Coleman remained with her fellow soldiers in country. Just over a month later, Coleman was on a foot patrol when another IED detonated beneath her. The explosion caused another TBI, internal damage, and tore off her left leg.

She survived these blasts and returned home, becoming medically retired from the Army. In 2012, the non-profit Helping A Hero donated a new, specially adapted home to Coleman and her husband in honor of her service and sacrifice.

TOMORROW, America finally says thank you. 🇺🇸

Thirty-five years after Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm, the National Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial will be dedicated tomorrow — Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. — at Constitution Avenue and 23rd Street NW in Washington, D.C., in the shadow of the Lincoln Memorial.

Nearly 700,000 American service members deployed to the Persian Gulf in 1990 and 1991. In just 100 hours of ground combat, the coalition liberated Kuwait in one of the most decisive victories in military history. But 382 Americans never came home — and for 35 years, their war had no national memorial in the capital. Until now.

The memorial's curving walls, carved from desert-colored stone, carry the images of the soldiers who fought there — including the great bas-relief wall in this photograph, with troops advancing forever across the stone. A 28-foot bronze Unity Shield bears the names of the coalition nations beneath cascading water, watched over by two sculptures: a bald eagle for America, and a falcon for Kuwait, created by veteran and sculptor Robert Eccleston.

Tomorrow, Desert Storm veterans and Gold Star families from across the nation will gather as the memorial is unveiled — including mothers who have waited 35 years for a place in Washington where their sons' and daughters' war is remembered.

They answered the call in the desert. Tomorrow, America answers back.

If you cannot attend, the dedication will be livestreamed at ndswm.org.

Julie Rochelle Hickey was born January 17, 1984, and grew up in Galloway, Ohio. She enlisted in the Army Reserve in October 2001 and completed the Civil Affairs Specialist Course at Fort Bragg. She later deployed to Afghanistan with the 401st Civil Affairs Battalion and served with a Provincial Reconstruction Team in Asadabad.

During her deployment, Hickey provided humanitarian assistance to Afghan people, particularly women and children. Congressional records describe her speaking to women's organizations about their rights, while her family recalled her work at a medical clinic, where she helped children and taught basic hygiene and some English. During leave in May 2004, she brought home a burqa given to her by an Afghan woman she had worked with.

After becoming ill while on duty in Asadabad, Hickey was moved to Bagram and later evacuated to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany on June 30, 2004. She d*ed there on July 4 from a non-combat-related illness. She was 20 years old. Her awards included the Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary Medal, Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, National Defense Service Medal, and Army Service Ribbon.
